name: Classic Rock
blurb: Arena anthems, guitar heroes and the albums that defined the AM and FM dial.

questions.prompt: Which band made Rumours (1977) while two of its couples were breaking up?
questions.fact: Rumours won the Grammy for Album of the Year. John and Christine McVie divorced, and Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks split, all during the sessions.

questions.prompt: Which guitarist closed the 1969 Woodstock festival on Monday morning with a Star-Spangled Banner?
questions.fact: By the time Hendrix played, much of the crowd had left, but his feedback-drenched anthem became one of the defining images of the 1960s.

questions.prompt: Woodstock was held on the farm of which dairy farmer in Bethel, New York?
questions.fact: Yasgur rented his land to the organizers after other towns turned them away, and famously told the crowd they had proved a half million people could enjoy themselves.

questions.prompt: Which Queen guitarist later earned a PhD in astrophysics?
questions.fact: May began the doctoral work at Imperial College in the early 1970s, set it aside for Queen, and completed his thesis in 2007.

questions.prompt: Cream was Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and which drummer?
questions.fact: The trio gave their farewell concerts at London's Royal Albert Hall in November 1968, just two and a half years after forming.

questions.prompt: Which Aerosmith guitarist and Steven Tyler were nicknamed the Toxic Twins?
questions.fact: Perry and Tyler's 1986 collaboration with Run-DMC on "Walk This Way" helped relaunch Aerosmith's career.

questions.prompt: Which Led Zeppelin drummer died in September 1980, prompting the band to break up?
questions.fact: Bonham died after a day of heavy drinking at Jimmy Page's home in Windsor. The surviving members announced in December that they could not continue.

questions.prompt: Whose saxophone shares the cover of Springsteen's Born to Run with him?
questions.fact: Photographer Eric Meola shot the cover. Springsteen leans on the "Big Man" Clemons, whose sax solo drives "Jungleland" and "Thunder Road".

questions.prompt: Which Queen song, built on stomps and claps with no drums or bass, was written by Brian May?
questions.fact: The stomp-stomp-clap was recorded at Wessex Studios, a converted church in north London, using layered foot stomps and hand claps.

questions.prompt: Which Led Zeppelin guitarist famously played his guitar with a violin bow on "Dazed and Confused"?
questions.fact: The bowed-guitar passage became a centerpiece of Zeppelin's live shows and ran for many minutes in concert versions.

questions.prompt: "Gimme Shelter" opens which 1969 Rolling Stones album?
questions.fact: Guest singer Merry Clayton's searing vocal on the song was recorded late at night in Los Angeles after she was called in as a favor.

questions.prompt: "Baba O'Riley" takes half its title from composer Terry Riley and which Indian spiritual teacher?
questions.fact: Pete Townshend, a follower of Meher Baba, built the song's pulsing synthesizer pattern from a Lifehouse project that was never finished as planned.

questions.prompt: The famous twin-guitar solo that closes "Hotel California" pairs Don Felder with which Eagle?
questions.fact: Felder wrote the original musical demo, and Walsh, who joined in 1975, traded the harmonized lines with him on the recording.

questions.prompt: Steppenwolf took its name from a novel by which author?
questions.fact: The band's "Born to Be Wild" gave rock the phrase "heavy metal thunder" in its lyrics.

questions.prompt: Which song is the 11-minute-plus closer of the Doors' 1967 debut album?
questions.fact: The Oedipal spoken section got the band thrown out of the Whisky a Go Go, and the song later opened Francis Ford Coppola's Apocalypse Now.

questions.prompt: The cover of Who's Next shows the band beside what object?
choices: A concrete monolith on a slag heap
questions.fact: The photo was taken at a slag heap near Easington Colliery in County Durham, and the pillar echoes the monolith in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

questions.prompt: Eric Clapton wrote "Layla" about Pattie Boyd, who was then married to which Beatle?
questions.fact: The title came from the Persian poem Layla and Majnun, and Duane Allman's slide guitar defines the song. Boyd later married Clapton.

questions.prompt: Which friend co-wrote the Eagles' first single, "Take It Easy"?
questions.fact: Browne started the song, and his neighbor Glenn Frey finished it, adding the line about the girl in a flatbed Ford. Winslow, Arizona, now has a statue honoring the song.

questions.prompt: The cover photograph of Hotel California shows which famous Beverly Hills landmark?
questions.fact: Photographer David Alexander shot the hotel at sunset, and the pink building has been tied to the album ever since.

questions.prompt: Who replaced Mick Taylor as the Rolling Stones' guitarist in 1975?
questions.fact: Wood had played with Rod Stewart in the Faces and the Jeff Beck Group, and he remains with the Stones today.

questions.prompt: Before they joined Fleetwood Mac, Buckingham and Nicks played in which band in the Bay Area?
questions.fact: Fritz, the Bay Area band where they met, reportedly opened shows for acts such as Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin. Mick Fleetwood later heard the duo's 1973 album Buckingham Nicks at Sound City and invited Buckingham to join, on the condition that Nicks come too.

questions.prompt: Boston's debut-album demos were recorded by Tom Scholz where?
questions.fact: The tape that won the contract was built in Scholz's home studio, where he also designed his own equipment. The demos became much of the 1976 album.

questions.prompt: Which London DJ played "Bohemian Rhapsody" 14 times over a weekend in 1975, helping force the label to release it?
questions.fact: Everett had been given an advance copy by Freddie Mercury, and EMI had worried that a six-minute single was too long for radio.

questions.prompt: Mark Knopfler's "Sultans of Swing" was inspired by a band he saw playing in a pub in which London district?
questions.fact: He has said the band played on to a nearly empty room, and the song's dry humor comes from that scene.

questions.prompt: "Maggie May" was originally released as the B-side of which Rod Stewart single?
questions.fact: A DJ flipped the single in 1971, and Ray Jackson of Lindisfarne played the mandolin, reportedly without credit on the first pressings.

questions.prompt: Paul Rodgers fronted which band before he co-founded Bad Company in 1973?
questions.fact: Bad Company's lineup also included Free drummer Simon Kirke, Mott the Hoople guitarist Mick Ralphs and King Crimson bassist Boz Burrell.

questions.prompt: Which band did Brian May and Roger Taylor play in before they met Freddie Mercury?
questions.fact: Smile's singer and bassist Tim Staffell left in 1970, and Mercury, a fan of the band, stepped in and renamed it Queen.

questions.prompt: Which band played Woodstock before its debut album had been released?
questions.fact: The San Francisco band's fiery "Soul Sacrifice" set made them stars. Their self-titled debut came out a couple of weeks later, at the end of August 1969.

questions.prompt: Which Fleetwood Mac singer duets with Tom Petty on "Stop Draggin' My Heart Around"?
questions.fact: Petty and guitarist Mike Campbell wrote the song, and producer Jimmy Iovine, who was working on Nicks's solo debut Bella Donna, brought the two stars together.

questions.prompt: What was Mick Jagger carrying when Keith Richards recognized him on a train platform in 1961?
choices: Records by Chuck Berry and Muddy Waters
questions.fact: The two had been schoolmates, and their shared taste for American blues gave them a reason to start a band.

questions.prompt: The cover of Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon shows a beam of light passing through what?
questions.fact: The sleeve was designed by Storm Thorgerson and Hipgnosis, and the prism and spectrum image became one of rock's best-known covers.

questions.prompt: Which Who drummer was known for smashing his kit on stage and died in September 1978?
questions.fact: Moon died at 32, and Kenney Jones took over the drum seat.

questions.prompt: The Who's rock opera Tommy centers on a boy who becomes a champion at what?
questions.fact: Released in 1969, Tommy produced "Pinball Wizard" and was later made into a 1975 film.

questions.prompt: Which Eagle sang lead on "Hotel California"?
questions.fact: Henley wrote it with Don Felder and Glenn Frey, and sang it on the 1976 album.

questions.prompt: The first pressings of the Rolling Stones' Sticky Fingers came with what working feature on the sleeve?
questions.fact: The 1971 cover concept is credited to Andy Warhol and showed a jeans zipper that really opened.

questions.prompt: Steppenwolf's "Born to Be Wild" was part of the soundtrack of which 1969 road movie?
questions.fact: Songwriter Mars Bonfire, brother of the band's drummer, wrote it, and its line about heavy metal thunder is often cited as an early use of the term.

questions.prompt: "Eye of the Tiger" was written for which 1982 movie?
questions.fact: Sylvester Stallone reportedly wanted a different song first, then asked Survivor to write one for the film.

questions.prompt: Which songwriter wrote "All Along the Watchtower", which Jimi Hendrix turned into a classic in 1968?
questions.fact: Dylan released it on John Wesley Harding in late 1967, and he has since played it in an arrangement close to Hendrix's.

questions.prompt: Much of Led Zeppelin IV was recorded in an English country house using which band's mobile studio?
questions.fact: Sessions at Headley Grange, a former workhouse in Hampshire, used the Stones' mobile unit, which reportedly helped give the drums a huge room sound.

questions.prompt: Joe Walsh joined the Eagles in 1975 to replace which founding member?
questions.fact: Leadon left after One of These Nights, and Walsh brought a harder guitar edge to Hotel California.

questions.prompt: Fleetwood Mac began in 1967 as a British blues band led by which guitarist?
questions.fact: Green named the group for the rhythm section of Mick Fleetwood and John McVie, and left in 1970.

questions.prompt: Which pop star reportedly urged Queen to release "Another One Bites the Dust" as a single?
questions.fact: The story goes that he saw the band in Los Angeles in 1980 and pushed for it, and John Deacon had written the bass riff.

questions.prompt: Pink Floyd's Wish You Were Here (1975) is widely seen as a tribute to which former bandmate?
questions.fact: Barrett reportedly turned up at the Abbey Road sessions looking so changed that the band barely recognized him.

questions.prompt: Cream's farewell concerts in November 1968 were played at which London hall?
questions.fact: The shows were filmed, and Ginger Baker, Jack Bruce and Eric Clapton went their separate ways soon after.

questions.prompt: In 1979, Tom Petty took what unusual legal step in a fight over his record contract?
choices: He signed with a rival label
questions.fact: A label sale had moved his contract to a new company, and the standoff came right before Damn the Torpedoes.

questions.prompt: "Baba O'Riley" was meant for an unfinished Pete Townshend project called what?
questions.fact: Lifehouse was a sci-fi rock opera idea that was never completed, but several of its songs ended up on Who's Next.

questions.prompt: Brian May built his Red Special guitar with his father, using wood from what?
questions.fact: The neck is reportedly made from a fireplace mantel, and the pair began work on it in the early 1960s.

questions.prompt: Joe Walsh's "Rocky Mountain Way" features a guitar effect that shapes the sound with the player's mouth. What is it?
questions.fact: Walsh used a talk box on the 1973 track, and the effect later became a signature of Peter Frampton's records too.

questions.prompt: Jim Morrison and Ray Manzarek first met as students in which university's film program?
questions.fact: Manzarek has said he heard Morrison sing a few lines on a beach in Venice, which led to forming the Doors.

questions.prompt: Boston founder Tom Scholz worked as a product designer for which company while building the first demos?
questions.fact: The MIT-trained Scholz recorded the early tracks in his basement, and much of the debut grew out of those demos.

songs.note: Keyboardist Ray Manzarek's Vox organ riff opens the song, and guitarist Robby Krieger wrote most of the lyrics.

songs.title: Baba O'Riley
songs.note: Its synthesizer loop opens the album and later the song became a stadium staple.

songs.note: The band's debut single was co-written by Jackson Browne and Glenn Frey.

songs.title: Can't Get Enough
songs.note: The band recorded its debut at Headley Grange, the country house where Led Zeppelin had made records, and Mick Ralphs wrote this song.

songs.title: Hotel California
songs.note: Don Felder wrote the music on a demo, and Don Henley and Glenn Frey wrote lyrics about the excess of Southern California.

songs.title: Dreams
songs.note: Stevie Nicks has said she wrote it in minutes, sitting on the bed in a small studio room at the Record Plant in Sausalito.

songs.title: Refugee

songs.note: John Deacon wrote the bass line, which was inspired by the funk band Chic.

songs.note: Tom Scholz built the demo in his basement studio near Boston, and the finished record kept much of that sound.

songs.title: Eye of the Tiger
songs.note: It was written for Rocky III at Sylvester Stallone's request.

stories.title: The Making of Rumours
stories.dek: Two broken couples, one hit album
stories.body:
In early 1976 Fleetwood Mac was a band in trouble that did not know it yet. Mick Fleetwood and John McVie were the rhythm section. Christine McVie was the keyboardist, John's wife, and one of the band's best songwriters. Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks had joined at the end of 1974, bringing California harmony and a romantic partnership. Their first album together, simply called Fleetwood Mac, had been a huge hit. The follow-up should have been a victory lap.

Instead, the personal lives fell apart as the band gathered at the Record Plant in Sausalito, California. The McVies' marriage was ending after eight years. Buckingham and Nicks, together for years, had also broken up. Fleetwood's own marriage was in trouble. Nobody left the band, and every day they walked into the same small studio to record songs about each other.

The results were frank. Buckingham wrote "Go Your Own Way" as a farewell to Nicks, and Nicks objected to the line about "shacking up". Christine McVie sang "Don't Stop" to her ex-husband and "You Make Loving Fun" about a new love. Nicks wrote "Dreams" in a short burst of inspiration, working in a small room in the studio, and "Gold Dust Woman" captured the darker moods of those weeks.

The sessions were long, and the band was known to work late into the night, with a lot of cocaine and alcohol around. They obsessed over details, redoing guitar parts and vocals until they had them. Producers Ken Caillat and Richard Dashut spent months assembling the final tapes, and they used the same master reel so many times that it began to wear thin.

Rumours arrived in February 1977 and the response was immense. It spent 31 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard album chart, produced four Top 10 singles and won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 1978. It has sold tens of millions of copies worldwide, and it still sells today.

Part of the album's enduring pull comes from the human drama behind it. A listener in 1977 did not need to know the backstory, because the songs spelled out their own heartache. Yet knowing the story adds a layer, since the same people who sang the sad lines also had to play the next take together. The band later said the tension was part of the energy, and that the album might never have existed if they had been happier. Whatever the truth, Rumours remains a lesson in how pain can become polished pop craft.

stories.title: Layla in Miami
stories.dek: Clapton, Allman and a love he could not have
stories.body:
In 1970 Eric Clapton was in love with Pattie Boyd, the wife of his friend George Harrison. He had no way to tell her, so he wrote songs. That summer he formed a new band with American musicians from the Delaney and Bonnie tour: keyboardist Bobby Whitlock, bassist Carl Radle and drummer Jim Gordon. They called themselves Derek and the Dominos, and they headed to Criteria Studios in Miami to record with producer Tom Dowd, who had worked with Clapton in Cream.

Dowd happened to be working with the Allman Brothers Band at the same time. He told Clapton about a young slide guitarist called Duane Allman, and the two met when Clapton went to see the Allmans play in Miami. They talked and then jammed through the night. Clapton later described the connection as the sort of musical brotherhood he had always wanted.

Allman joined the sessions, and the pair played off each other like old partners. The title song was inspired by Layla and Majnun, the classic Persian poem of unattainable love, which a friend had given Clapton. Clapton wrote the main part of the song, and Allman's opening slide figure became one of the most famous riffs in rock. The band cut the first part of the song, then added a very different piano coda, a calm, melodic ending that gives the track its mood of exhaustion after a storm.

The album, Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs, appeared in November 1970. It was not an immediate success. Reviewers praised it, but the band was little known and the double-album format was a hard sell. The single "Layla" first reached only the middle of the US charts in 1971. After the band split and Clapton retreated into a long struggle with addiction, radio programmers kept playing the song, and when it was reissued in 1972 it climbed to the US Top 10.

Allman had returned to the Allman Brothers Band after the sessions. In October 1971 he was killed in a motorcycle accident in Macon, Georgia, at the age of 24. Clapton always said the finished song would not have existed without him. Boyd eventually left Harrison and married Clapton in 1979, though the marriage later ended. As for the song, it has had a long life, and in 1992 Clapton played a quiet acoustic version on MTV Unplugged that won him a Grammy. Layla still sounds like what it was: a message sent by a man who could not say it aloud.

stories.title: Six Minutes of Bohemian Rhapsody
stories.dek: The song that broke every rule
stories.body:
Queen's fourth album, A Night at the Opera, was a bold experiment in 1975. It cost a lot to record and had no particular style. The band wanted each song to be different. The centerpiece was a song Freddie Mercury had been carrying in his head for years, and which he finally brought to the others in pieces, playing the piano and singing the harmonies himself.

Mercury arrived with the song largely written out on scraps of paper. It had a ballad introduction, a guitar solo, an operatic middle and a hard rock ending. The recording took about three weeks, and it was done at several studios, including Rockfield in Wales. The opera section alone took days, because the singers, Mercury, Brian May and Roger Taylor, layered their voices again and again to sound like a giant choir. According to May, the tape was copied and overdubbed so many times that it became almost transparent.

Producer Roy Thomas Baker supported the plan, but the record company was worried. At nearly six minutes, the song was three times the usual length of a single, and radio stations rarely played anything that long. Mercury gave a copy to Kenny Everett, a friendly DJ at Capital Radio in London, who had promised not to play it. He played it anyway, reportedly more than a dozen times over a weekend. Listeners phoned in to ask where they could buy it, and the label had to release it.

The single came out in October 1975 and reached No. 1 in the UK, staying there for nine weeks over the Christmas period. The band also made a promotional film, directed by Bruce Gowers in a few hours at Elstree Studios, to promote the song on television. The clip, which opens with the four members' faces in a diamond, is often credited with helping to launch the music video era.

Critics were split at first. Some found the song bombastic and others a masterpiece, but listeners embraced it. Mercury never fully explained the lyrics, saying only that the song was about relationships, and he refused to give a simple meaning to the story of Galileo and the other figures. After his death in 1991, it returned to the top of the UK chart in early 1992. Few singles have stayed so popular for so long, or sounded so little like anything else on the radio.
